arise.verb type: action — dynamic, but with an abstract subject: problems, questions, and needs *arise*. No linking or stative use.
arise.transitivity: **intransitive** only, in every sense — *a dispute arose*, *claims arise from the accident*. You *raise* a question; ✗ *he arose the issue*.
arise.passive: **no** — there is no object to promote: ✗ *a dispute was arisen over the fence*. Only the active *a dispute arose* is possible.

befall.verb type: action — dynamic; the subject is an event or a misfortune, not a person who acts.
befall.transitivity: **transitive** in the living sense, with a person or place as the object — *a string of disasters befell the company*. The archaic sense 2 is **intransitive**: *it befell on the third night*.
befall.passive: **no** in practice — transitive but it resists promotion: ✗ *the company was befallen by disasters*. Keep the active, or switch to *was struck by*.

bequeath.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of transfer like *give*.
bequeath.transitivity: **ditransitive** — *that century bequeathed us the vaccine*, or with *to*: *her will bequeathed the house to her sister*.
bequeath.passive: **yes** — *the house was bequeathed to her sister*, and three paintings *have been bequeathed* to the museum.

bestride.verb type: action — dynamic in the literal *bestride a log*; closer to stative in the dominating sense, where it describes a standing position rather than an act.
bestride.transitivity: **transitive** in every sense, and the object is obligatory — *one firm bestrides the market*; ✗ *the general bestrode for years*.
bestride.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but rare and stiff: *the industry has been bestridden by one company* is possible in literary writing, though the active is far more natural.

bid.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from offering a price to commanding.
bid.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with a preposition in business (*they bid on federal jobs*), transitive with an amount (*she bid nine hundred dollars*), and ditransitive in the command and greeting senses (*she bade us good night*, *he bids his students think for themselves*).
bid.passive: **yes**, but sense by sense — *that lamp has been bid on twice*, *the guests had been bidden to arrive at seven*. The frozen *bid farewell* stays active: ✗ *farewell was bidden to us*.

blow.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, whether the subject is wind, a person, or a fuse.
blow.transitivity: **both** — intransitive of wind and of things that fail (*cold winds blow*, *the rear tire blew*), transitive when something is moved, sounded, or wasted (*the storm blew three shingles off*, *he blew a paycheck*).
blow.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the umbrella has been blown into the pool*, *the whistle was blown on the play*. No passive of the intransitive *the fuse blew*.

co-write.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of creation.
co-write.transitivity: **transitive** — the work is the object and the collaborator follows *with*: *she co-wrote the screenplay with her brother*. The object is normally obligatory.
co-write.passive: **yes**, and it is the usual form in credits — *the report had been co-written by two agencies*.

crow.verb type: action — dynamic; a verb of noise-making, both for the rooster and for the person gloating.
crow.transitivity: **intransitive** in all three senses; the thing boasted about follows *about* or *over*: *he crowed about the promotion*. ✗ *he crowed his win*.
crow.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the promotion was crowed about* is at best marginal, and ✗ *the win was crowed*.

do.verb type: **both lexical and auxiliary** — an action verb in *do the dishes*, and the tense-carrying **auxiliary** of questions, negatives, and emphasis (*do you take cream?*, *I do remember*), plus a pro-verb standing in for an earlier verb (*she reads more than I do*).
do.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the lexical senses (*do the dishes*, *do thirty miles to the gallon*), intransitive in *that will do* and *she has done well*. The auxiliary takes no object at all.
do.passive: **yes** in the lexical transitive senses — *the upstairs has been done already*, *the essay had to be done over*. The auxiliary and pro-verb uses have no passive: ✗ *cream is done taken by you*.

draw.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from making lines to attracting a crowd.
draw.transitivity: **both** — transitive in most senses (*she drew a map*, *free food draws a crowd*, *you can draw cash*), intransitive in *architects still draw by hand*, in the sports *United drew with City*, and in *winter draws near*.
draw.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the curtains had been drawn*, *the exhibit's crowds were drawn by the reviews*, *new rules have been drawn up*. No passive of *winter draws near*.

drive.verb type: action — dynamic; the subject is either an operator or a force.
drive.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in *he drove nine hours*, transitive with a vehicle, a person, a nail, or a herd (*drive the stake in*, *I can drive you to the airport*), and with an object plus a resultant complement in *the noise drives me crazy*.
drive.passive: **yes** — *the pumps have been driven by solar panels since June*, *young families have been driven out of the city*. No passive of the intransitive *he drove nine hours*.

eat.verb type: action — dynamic, including the figurative *rust ate through the pan*.
eat.transitivity: **both**, with an optional object — *we eat dinner around seven* and plain *the kids have eaten already* are equally good. Transitive in *rent eats up half her paycheck*.
eat.passive: **yes** where there is an object — *every roll had been eaten by the time I sat down*, *the settlement has been eaten up by legal fees*. No passive of *they ate out*.

fall.verb type: action — dynamic; also **linking (copular)** in the fixed *fall asleep, fall ill, fall silent, fall in love*, where an adjective or phrase follows instead of an object.
fall.transitivity: **intransitive** in every sense, and this is the trap: ✗ *he fell the glass* — you *drop* a glass, or *fell* a tree with the separate regular verb *fell, felled*.
fall.passive: **no** — nothing can be promoted: ✗ *the capital was fallen in three days*. *The fallen* is a noun from the participle, not a passive.

fly.verb type: action — dynamic, of birds, aircraft, time, and tempers.
fly.transitivity: **both** — intransitive of motion (*geese fly south*, *we flew to Denver*, *time flies*), transitive when you pilot or hoist something (*she flies cargo runs*, *ships fly the flag*) or flee a place (*he flew the country*).
fly.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the flag has been flown at half staff all week*, *the last leg was flown by the copilot*. No passive of *we flew to Denver*.

forbid.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of ordering; the subject can also be an inanimate rule or law.
forbid.transitivity: **transitive**, with a personal object plus *to* or *from* (*forbade him to leave*, *forbade him from leaving*) or with a bare object (*most parks forbid open fires*). Never a bare infinitive: ✗ *forbade him leave*.
forbid.passive: **yes**, and the participle is everywhere as an adjective — *subletting is forbidden by the lease*, *he was forbidden to leave the state*.

foresee.verb type: **stative** — a mental verb of knowing in advance, so it stays out of the progressive: ✗ *I am foreseeing trouble*; say *I foresee trouble*.
foresee.transitivity: **transitive**, with a noun or a clause as the object — *few economists foresee a sharp drop*, *nobody foresaw how fast it would change*.
foresee.passive: **yes** — unusual for a stative verb, but natural here: *the flaw had been foreseen but overruled*, *a delay that long could not have been foreseen*.

forgive.verb type: action — dynamic; a change of attitude rather than a state, so the progressive is fine (*she is forgiving him slowly*).
forgive.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in *some people forgive easily*, transitive with a person or a debt (*she forgave him*, *the bank forgave the loan*), and ditransitive in the older *forgive us our debts*.
forgive.passive: **yes** — *part of the loan has been forgiven*, *he was never really forgiven for it*.

forsake.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of abandoning; formal and literary in register.
forsake.transitivity: **transitive** in both senses, and the object is obligatory — *he forsook the city*, *good friends do not forsake you*. ✗ *her sons had forsaken* on its own.
forsake.passive: **yes** — *the valley had been forsaken by 1890*. The participle also stands alone as an adjective: *a forsaken little town*.

give.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, including the intransitive *the floorboard gave under his weight*. The participle *given* has hardened into a preposition in *given the weather*.
give.transitivity: **ditransitive** in the core sense, either order — *he gave me his number* / *he gave his number to me*. Also plain transitive (*they gave a party*) and intransitive (*alumni give to the fund*, *the old lock gives*).
give.passive: **yes**, and either object can be promoted — *she was given the keys already* or *the keys were given to her*. No passive of *the floorboard gave*.

grow.verb type: action — dynamic; also **linking (copular)** in sense 4, where an adjective follows: *grow tired*, *grow dark*, *the crowd has grown quiet*.
grow.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when something gets bigger on its own (*the town has grown by half*), transitive when you cultivate or expand something (*she grows herbs*, *he has grown revenue every quarter*, *grow a beard*).
grow.passive: **yes** in the cultivate and expand senses — *the same corn has been grown here for forty years*. No passive of the intransitive *the town grew* or of the linking *it grew dark*.

know.verb type: **stative** — a verb of cognition, and one of the clearest cases of a verb that rejects the progressive: ✗ *I am knowing the answer*; say *I know the answer*.
know.transitivity: **transitive**, with a noun, a clause, or *how to* as the object — *they know the neighborhood*, *she knew how to fix the pump*. Weakened with a preposition in *I know of her*.
know.passive: **restricted** — stative, so the plain passive is bad: ✗ *the answer is known by me*. It survives in fixed frames with no *by*-phrase: *the street is known for its bakeries*, *he was known around town as Doc*, *the place has been known by three names*.

lie.verb type: **stative** in the situated and remaining senses (*the town lies east of the river*, *the mill lay idle*) — closer to a position than an act; **action** only in the moment of lying down. The *lie idle / lie empty* pattern is effectively **linking**.
lie.transitivity: **intransitive** in every sense. Its transitive twin is the separate regular *lay, laid, laid*: you *lay* a book down, but ✗ *I laid down for a nap* — the past of *lie* is *lay*: *I lay down for a nap*.
lie.passive: **no** — no object exists to promote: ✗ *the counter was lain on by the keys*. Only the active *the keys have lain on the counter*.

mistake.verb type: action — dynamic but mental, a verb of misidentifying; the progressive is rare outside *there is no mistaking that voice*.
mistake.transitivity: **transitive**, in the fixed frame *mistake A for B* — *I mistook the salt for sugar*. Never *mistake A with B*.
mistake.passive: **yes** — *she is often mistaken for her sister*. The fixed *you are mistaken* looks passive but the participle there is a plain adjective meaning *wrong*.

outdo.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of surpassing.
outdo.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory — a rival, a previous version, or a reflexive: *nobody outdoes him at trivia*, *she outdid herself with the cake*. ✗ *the sequel has outdone* alone.
outdo.passive: **yes**, though mostly in the frozen *not to be outdone* — *the original has been outdone at the box office* is fine but less common than the active.

outgrow.verb type: action — dynamic; the change is gradual, but it is still something that happens rather than a state.
outgrow.transitivity: **transitive** in every sense, and the object is obligatory — *kids outgrow shoes*, *the company had outgrown its first office*. ✗ *he has outgrown from his fear*.
outgrow.passive: **restricted** — natural enough with institutions (*the building had been outgrown within a year*), stiff with clothes and phases: ? *every coat we bought her has been outgrown*.

overdo.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of excess.
overdo.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory — most often the empty *it* (*don't overdo it*), otherwise an ingredient or an effect (*he overdid the garlic*, *the script overdid the sentiment*).
overdo.passive: **yes** — *every burger on the tray has been overdone*. The participle is an ordinary adjective too: *an overdone steak*.

overdraw.verb type: action — dynamic; in banking, an act with a consequence, and in criticism, a way of portraying.
overdraw.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the account or the character as the object (*he overdrew the account by sixty dollars*), intransitive in *the app warns you before you overdraw*.
overdraw.passive: **yes**, and this is how most Americans meet the word — *the account was overdrawn when the check cleared*, *every figure in the book has been overdrawn*.

overeat.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of excess built on *eat*.
overeat.transitivity: **intransitive** only — ✗ *I overate the pie*; say *I ate too much pie* or simply *I overate*.
overeat.passive: **no** — intransitive, so nothing can be promoted: ✗ *the pie was overeaten*.

overgrow.verb type: action — dynamic in the finite forms, though in practice Americans meet only the participle *overgrown* used as an adjective (*an overgrown lot*, *an overgrown puppy*).
overgrow.transitivity: **transitive** — the plant is the subject and the surface is the object: *ivy has overgrown the north wall*.
overgrow.passive: **yes**, and it is the usual form — *the fence is overgrown with vines*, *the yard was completely overgrown*, where the participle also reads as a plain adjective.

overlie.verb type: **stative** in the geological sense — a description of how layers sit, not an event: *sandstone overlies the coal seam*. **Action** only in the narrow *smother by lying on* sense.
overlie.transitivity: **transitive** in both senses, unlike its base verb *lie* — *volcanic rock has overlain these deposits*, *the sow overlay two of the piglets*.
overlie.passive: **yes**, and standard in geology — *the coal seam is overlain by sandstone throughout the valley*. Rare and awkward in the smothering sense.

override.verb type: action — dynamic; in sense 2 the subject is abstract (*safety concerns override the schedule*) but the verb still names an event.
override.transitivity: **transitive** in every sense, and the object is obligatory — *the Senate can override a veto*, *subclasses override the default constructor*.
override.passive: **yes** — *the store policy has been overridden twice this month*, *someone had overridden the alarm*.

oversee.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of supervising; unlike its base *see* it takes the progressive freely (*she is overseeing the renovation*).
oversee.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory — *two engineers oversee the assembly line*. ✗ *a monitor had overseen for three years*.
oversee.passive: **yes** — *the department had been overseen by a federal monitor for three years*, *clinical trials like this have been overseen by the agency for decades*.

overtake.verb type: action — dynamic, whether the subject is a car, a sales figure, or a blizzard.
overtake.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory — *a gray sedan overtook us*, *online orders have overtaken walk-in business*. ✗ *the lorry overtook on the bend* takes an object in the British driving use too, though *no overtaking* is a fixed sign.
overtake.passive: **yes**, and sense 3 is usually passive — *the expedition was overtaken by a blizzard*, *their plan had been overtaken by events*.

overthrow.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of removing by force.
overthrow.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory — a government, a theory, or, in sports, the target of a throw: *the shortstop overthrew first base*.
overthrow.passive: **yes**, and the political sense is very often passive — *the monarchy has been overthrown twice in a single century*, *his receiver had been overthrown on three straight plays*.

overwrite.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of replacing.
overwrite.transitivity: **transitive** in the data and manuscript senses (*the installer overwrote my custom settings*); in sense 3 it is used both transitively (*don't overwrite a simple scene*) and absolutely (*first novels are overwritten*).
overwrite.passive: **yes**, and it is routine in computing — *last night's export has been overwritten with an empty file*, *the middle chapters were badly overwritten*.

partake.verb type: action — dynamic in the eating and taking-part senses; closer to **stative** in the formal sense 3, where something shares a quality: *his speeches partake of the sermon*.
partake.transitivity: **intransitive** — it always needs a preposition, *of* for food and qualities, *in* for activities. ✗ *partake the meal*; say *partake of the meal*.
partake.passive: **no** — there is no direct object to promote: ✗ *the buffet was partaken of by the guests*. Keep the active, or use *take part in*.

redraw.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of doing again.
redraw.transitivity: **transitive** in the drawing and boundary senses (*legislatures redraw congressional districts*); **intransitive** with *on* in the banking sense: *the bank redrew on its correspondent in London*.
redraw.passive: **yes** — *congressional districts are redrawn after every census*, *the second floor had been redrawn twice by Friday*.

regrow.verb type: action — dynamic, of growth returning after loss.
regrow.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when the thing comes back on its own (*her hair regrew within a year*), transitive when someone makes it come back (*you can regrow scallions from the roots*).
regrow.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the cartilage was regrown on a printed scaffold*. No passive of the intransitive *the prairie grass has regrown*.

retake.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of taking again.
retake.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory — *allied forces retook the port*, *he retook chemistry over the summer*, *they retook the final shot*.
retake.passive: **yes** — *the port was retaken in a single night*, *the exam can be retaken once*.

rewrite.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of producing a new version.
rewrite.transitivity: **transitive**, with a text, a rule, or a body of code as the object — *she rewrote the ending*, *they rewrote the backend in Go*.
rewrite.passive: **yes** — *the rules have been rewritten three times this year*, *that module has been rewritten from scratch twice*.

ride.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, including the fixed *a lot of money is riding on the outcome*, which lives almost entirely in the progressive.
ride.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in *she rides every Saturday*, transitive with an animal, a vehicle, a wave, or a person (*he rode his motorcycle*, *I ride the train*, *the coach rode the rookies*). Prepositional in *riding on* and *ride out*.
ride.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *that gray mare has been ridden since she was three*, *this break has been ridden since the fifties*. No passive of *she rides every Saturday*.

rise.verb type: action — dynamic, of upward movement, increase, and advancement.
rise.transitivity: **intransitive** only, in every sense — the counterpart *raise* (regular: *raised, raised*) is the transitive one. ✗ *he rose the flag*; say *he raised the flag* or *the flag rose*.
rise.passive: **no** — nothing to promote: ✗ *the water was risen over the doorsill*. Only the active *the water had risen over the doorsill*.

see.verb type: **stative** in the core perception and understanding senses, so it normally avoids the progressive: ✗ *I am seeing three deer*. The dating sense is the exception and is **dynamic**: *they have been seeing each other since March*.
see.transitivity: **transitive** with a noun, a clause, or a bare infinitive or -ing complement — *I saw him leave*, *I saw him leaving*, never ✗ *I saw him to leave*. Prepositional in *see to it that*.
see.passive: **yes** — unusually for a stative verb, it passivizes freely: *that comet has not been seen since 1997*, *the film was seen as an apology for the war*.

shake.verb type: action — dynamic, of literal motion and of emotional jolts alike.
shake.transitivity: **both** — transitive when you move something (*shake the bottle well*, *he shook the sand out*) or unsettle someone (*the accident shook the crew*), intransitive when the subject trembles on its own (*my hands shake*, *the whole house shook*).
shake.passive: **yes**, and the emotional sense is very often passive — *her confidence has been shaken by two rejections*, *the last apples have been shaken loose*. No passive of *the house shook*.

slay.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses.
slay.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the killing and the *you slay me* senses (*he slew the giant*, *her set slew the crowd*), intransitive in the modern slang: *they absolutely slayed*.
slay.passive: **yes** for the killing sense, where the passive is the commonest form — *thousands had been slain before the treaty*, *four slain in crash*. No passive of the intransitive slang *she slays every time*.

smite.verb type: action — dynamic; archaic in the finite forms, and today alive mainly as the participle *smitten* used as an adjective meaning infatuated.
smite.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is a person, an enemy, or a place: *he smote the table with his fist*, *plague can smite a whole village*.
smite.passive: **yes**, and modern use is almost entirely passive — *he was smitten with her from the first rehearsal*, *the region has been smitten by drought three years running*.

stride.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of manner of walking; it carries purpose, so you do not *stride* aimlessly.
stride.transitivity: **intransitive** in the living senses, usually with a direction or a preposition — *she strode to the front of the room*, *he strode over the fallen branch*. The rare literary sense 3 takes an object: *the colossus strode the harbor mouth*.
stride.passive: **no** in the ordinary walking senses — ✗ *the lobby had been stridden across*. Even the transitive sense 3 resists it, and writers rephrase around the stiff participle *stridden*.

strive.verb type: action — dynamic, of sustained effort over time.
strive.transitivity: **intransitive** — it takes *to* plus a verb, *for* plus a goal, or *against* plus an obstacle, never a plain object: ✗ *she strove accuracy*; say *she strove for accuracy*.
strive.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *accuracy was striven for by her* is at best stilted. Keep the active.

take.verb type: action — dynamic across its whole range, including the light-verb uses (*take a look*, *take a break*) where the meaning sits in the noun.
take.transitivity: **transitive** in nearly every sense, and the object is obligatory — ✗ *she took* alone. **Ditransitive** in the carrying sense (*I take the kids their lunch*), and it takes an object plus a complement in *they took his silence as agreement*.
take.passive: **yes** — *my umbrella has been taken from the stand*, *the accounts will be taken over in the fall*. The requirement sense resists it: ✗ *twenty minutes is taken to get downtown*.

test-drive.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of trying out.
test-drive.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory — *we test-drove three hybrids*, *let's test-drive the new scheduling tool*.
test-drive.passive: **yes** — *that model has been test-driven by half the neighborhood*, *two workflows have been test-driven this month*.

thrive.verb type: action — dynamic in that it describes ongoing flourishing rather than a fixed state, and it takes the progressive freely: *the shop is thriving*.
thrive.transitivity: **intransitive** — the thing you flourish because of follows *on*: *she thrived on deadlines*. ✗ *he thrives pressure*.
thrive.passive: **no** — intransitive, so no passive exists: ✗ *deadlines were thriven on by her*. Only the active *she thrived on deadlines*.

throw.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from a pitch to hosting a party to unsettling a witness.
throw.transitivity: **transitive** in most senses (*he threw the ball*, *they throw a block party*, *the change of venue threw the team*), **ditransitive** in *we threw her a surprise dinner*, and **intransitive** in *he threw up twice*.
throw.passive: **yes** — *the entire complaint has been thrown out*, *a brick had been thrown through the window*. The idiom *throw up* has no passive: ✗ *lunch was thrown up*.

underbid.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of bidding.
underbid.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a rival or a hand as the object (*two firms tried to underbid us*, *she underbade a hand worth an easy game*), intransitive in *cautious partners underbid out of habit*.
underbid.passive: **yes** — *we have been underbidden on every municipal job this year*, though ordinary American business English would say *we were underbid*.

underlie.verb type: **stative** — it names a relation of one thing to another, not an event, and it stays out of the progressive: ✗ *two assumptions are underlying the proposal*; say *two assumptions underlie the proposal*.
underlie.transitivity: **transitive**, unlike its base verb *lie* — *old resentments underlay the whole dispute*, *limestone beds underlie most of the county*.
underlie.passive: **restricted** — standard and common in the geological sense (*the site is underlain by solid granite*), stiff in the abstract one, where writers reach for the adjective instead: *the underlying cause*.

undertake.verb type: action — dynamic, of taking on a task or making a commitment.
undertake.transitivity: **transitive** with a substantial object (*the agency will undertake a full review*), or with *to* plus a verb in the promising sense (*he undertook to repay the loan*). The archaic funeral sense is intransitive: *the same firm undertook for most of the county*.
undertake.passive: **yes** — *three studies have been undertaken on the same question*, *the largest survey in its history had been undertaken by spring*.

underwrite.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of assuming risk or paying for something.
underwrite.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory — a policy, an issue, or an event: *two banks will underwrite the offering*.
underwrite.passive: **yes**, and it is the natural form in finance — *the offering was underwritten by two banks*, *this station has been underwritten by listeners since 1974*.

undo.verb type: action — dynamic, of unfastening and of reversing. The participle *undone* doubles as an adjective: *his shoelace came undone*.
undo.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory — *he undid the top button*, *that single email undid six months of goodwill*. The fixed *come undone* uses *come*, not *undo*.
undo.passive: **yes**, and the fixed negative passive is everywhere — *the damage cannot be undone*, *someone has undone the latch*, *the twine had been undone*.

withdraw.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, including the psychological *he withdrew into his work*.
withdraw.transitivity: **both** — transitive with money, a statement, or troops (*she withdrew the whole balance*, *the company withdrew its offer*), intransitive with *from* (*he withdrew from the tournament*, *patients should not withdraw abruptly*).
withdraw.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *two of the charges have been withdrawn*, *the forward units were withdrawn overnight*. No passive of *he withdrew from the tournament*.

write.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of creation and of recording.
write.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in *he writes for two magazines*, transitive with a text or a document (*she wrote her first novel*), and **ditransitive** in American English: *the clinic will write you a prescription*, *write me when you get settled*.
write.passive: **yes** — *the same phrase has been written on every page*, *the remaining balance was written off*, *she has been written up twice for being late*.
